html:
Industrialisation is the shift from hand work to machines, factories and fossil fuel that began in Britain around 1760 and spread to Europe and North America by about 1840. Historians call it the Industrial Revolution. For the first time, output per person kept rising for generations instead of falling back.

It started with cloth. New spinning and weaving machines, first driven by water and then by steam, made cotton cheap in the cotton revolution. The Watt steam engine of 1769 made steam power efficient enough to drive mills anywhere, burning coal. Better ways of making iron followed, and from 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway showed what steam could do for transport.

Why Britain came first is still debated. Common answers are cheap coal, high wages that made machines worth buying, Atlantic trade and colonies, and a large market at home.

  • Belgium, France and parts of Germany followed, then the United States.
  • People moved from farms to fast-growing, crowded cities. Child labour and long factory hours were common.
  • A second wave after about 1870 brought steel, electricity and chemistry, such as the Haber process.

Industry gave Europe and the United States a huge lead in wealth and weapons over the rest of the world, the gap historians call the Great Divergence. That gap stands behind the empires of the nineteenth century.
